\begin{abstract}
Does mandated climate adaptation pay for itself? I study the 1994 HUD wind standard reform, which required structural upgrades to manufactured homes in hurricane-prone areas. Homes built before the reform are in fixed supply and are close substitutes for homes built after it, so the resale price gap between the two vintages measures the value buyers place on the mandated resilience, while the cost of the standard raises the price of both. Using county-level property records, I find that post-reform homes in the highest-risk counties sell at a premium that is positive in every specification but imprecisely estimated: it cannot be distinguished from HUD's \emph{ex ante} forecast of private benefits and, in `r cl_static_p3_zero` of four specifications, cannot be distinguished from zero. Surviving quantities in the same counties fall by up to `r tex(cl_count_drop_z3)`, which implies that the cost of the standard exceeded the value buyers placed on it. Using claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), I compare flood damage to manufactured and site-built homes of different construction vintages exposed to floods in the same county and over the same period. Manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r tex(bldg_dmg_pct)` less building damage per claim relative to site-built homes of the same vintage. The present value of these benefits is small -- only `r cl_flood_pv` per insured home in Zone III -- reflecting the low values of insured manufactured homes: median reported building values in the claim sample are `r tex(mh_value_gap_pct)` lower than for site-built homes. For manufactured-home owners, mandatory climate adaptation does not generally pencil out.
\end{abstract}

# Introduction

The U.S. experienced over 100 billion-dollar climate disasters over the five years before 2026, incurring damages of over \$600 billion dollars.[^billion-dollar] These costs are projected to grow substantially as climate change intensifies extreme weather events. Building codes and other forms of mandated adaptation investment are a potential policy tool for reducing disaster losses and risk, but the returns to these investments are not well understood, and they may have indirect effects on household's exposure to climate risk by interacting with insurance markets. This paper provides new evidence on the costs and benefits of mandated adaptation in the context of manufactured housing (MH), a sector that is both highly vulnerable to climate risk and largely -- though not entirely -- uninsured.[^mh]

[^billion-dollar]: Climate Central. "U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters." ClimateCentral.Org, 2026. \href{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}.

[^mh]: "Manufactured homes" are the preferred industry term and refer specifically to mobile homes that satisfy the 1976 HUD Code. As the vast majority of mobile homes produced since 1976 satisfy the code, I use the terms "manufactured" and "mobile" interchangeably.

Government mandates for costly adaptation may be justified if private take-up is hindered by frictions. For instance, households may misperceive climate risk [@bakkensen_going_2022; @gallagher_learning_2014]. They may fail to internalize benefits to their neighbors [@baylis_mandated_2021]. They may enjoy limited upside from adaptation if mitigation behaviors are not reflected in insurance premiums [@wagner_adaptation_2022]. Finally, they may rely on public insurance programs and disaster relief instead [@deryugina_fiscal_2017; @baylis_moral_2019].

I estimate the reform's effects on manufactured-home resale prices and surviving quantities, alongside its benefits from reduced flood damage. I interpret the price and quantity evidence with a simple argument. Homes built to the pre-reform standard cannot be built after 1994, so their supply is fixed, and they are close substitutes for post-reform homes. New homes are supplied at their cost of production, which the standard raised. A buyer therefore pays for a post-reform home the price of a pre-reform home of the same age plus the present value of the resilience the standard adds. Three implications follow. First, the resale price gap between post- and pre-reform vintages in the same market measures the value buyers place on the added resilience, not the cost of the standard. Second, the cost increase, less that value, raises the price of all manufactured homes in the treated market, pre- and post-reform alike. Third, placements of new homes fall if and only if the cost increase exceeds the value buyers place on the added resilience. If buyers place no value on it, the vintage gap is zero and all manufactured-home prices in the treated market rise by the cost increase. Public insurance and disaster relief transfer part of the benefit of resilience from owners to the government, so the value to buyers can fall short of the social value.

On the price and quantity side, I use county-level property and transaction records to compare manufactured homes built before and after 1994 across HUD wind zones. The transaction prices include land and reflect the value of existing homes rather than the price of new construction. The main dynamic specifications include county $\times$ sale-year effects for prices (county effects for counts) and state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects. Static specifications also report common vintage effects and, for prices, use site-built homes as a further comparison. In Zone III, post-reform homes sell at a premium of `r lad_min("price", 3)` to `r lad_max("price", 3)` across specifications, equivalent to `r cl_premium_lo`--`r cl_premium_hi` at the pre-reform-vintage Zone III mean of `r cl_price_base` (2000 dollars). The premium is positive in every specification, but it is imprecisely estimated. Its 95\% interval contains HUD's \emph{ex ante} forecast of private benefits, `r cl_hud_private` per home, in every specification and contains zero in `r cl_static_p3_zero` of the four. Zone II has no robust price premium. Counts of surviving manufactured homes fall in both treated zones. Because improved resilience should raise survival, the decline understates the fall in placements, and it implies that the cost of the standard exceeded the value buyers placed on it. Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs} reports state-level Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) estimates. Their price and placement paths may partly reflect the expansion and contraction of chattel lending in the late 1990s, and state-level treatment cannot separate the standard from state-specific vintage profiles. The county-level design assigns treatment at the level where the standard varies and allows state-specific vintage profiles.

On the benefit side, I use flood insurance claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to estimate the effect of the HUD standard on flood damage. My identification strategy exploits two sources of variation: MH versus site-built housing, and post-1994 versus pre-1994 construction vintage. County by flood-loss-period fixed effects ensure comparisons are made only between homes exposed to the same floods in the same location. This is a double-difference in vintage and housing type: the site-built comparison group absorbs secular changes in construction quality and storm severity, isolating the manufactured-home-specific break at 1994.

Post-1994 manufactured homes experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim relative to pre-1994 manufactured homes, compared to the same vintage difference for site-built homes. The estimates are proportional rather than absolute, for reasons set out in Section \ref{results}: manufactured and site-built homes differ in value by a factor of roughly two and a half, and a specification in dollars is not identified in its own units when the effect it estimates is a percentage. Against a pre-1994 manufactured-home mean of `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim, the proportional estimate is `r bldg_dmg_eff`. The event study shows the effect emerging at 1994 and growing with later construction cohorts, consistent with delays between the manufacture and installation of MH, though the pre-1994 coefficients wander enough that the break is less sharp than the static estimate alone suggests. Contents damage falls by `r cont_dmg_pct` and contents payments by `r net_cont_pct`. At the same time, MH policies for post-1994 vintages are more likely to be located in Special Flood Hazard Areas, and carry higher replacement costs and building coverage, all of which would tend to increase expected NFIP payments. These compositional shifts run against the estimated damage reductions rather than producing them.

For a back-of-envelope comparison, I pair the Zone III resale premium with flood-benefit estimates for the same wind zone. Applying zone-specific proportional loss reductions to pre-1994 manufactured-home mean losses and the insured claim rate yields `r cl_flood_pv` in present-value avoided flood damage, discounting at `r hud_rate` over `r hud_life` years as in HUD's analysis. Of the avoided damage, `r cl_public_pv` accrues to the NFIP through reduced payments. The remaining `r cl_retained_pv` is the insured household's retained-loss benefit, which is one component of the value capitalized into the resale premium; it is `r cl_private_share` of the baseline premium of `r cl_premium`. The low value of manufactured homes limits these benefits. An upgrade that removes a given share of damage saves fewer dollars on a home worth less, while the cost of structural upgrades depends on the size of a home more than on its value. These comparisons condition on NFIP coverage and do not measure the full return to a wind standard.

At the aggregate level, the reform generates meaningful fiscal spillovers. The point estimates imply reductions of `r net_bldg_pct` in net building payments and `r net_cont_pct` in net contents payments per MH claim, or `r net_bldg_eff` and `r net_cont_eff` against the observed post-1994 manufactured-home means of `r mh_post_nbldg` and `r mh_post_ncont`. Applied to the `r n_post_claims` claims on MH built between 1994 and 1999 observed in the NFIP sample, this yields roughly `r nfip_sav_m` in direct NFIP payment savings---a conservative figure that conditions on filing a claim and does not scale to the full stock of post-reform MH.[^fiscal-nfip] Spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster relief---most notably FEMA Individual Assistance, SBA disaster loans, and state emergency grants---are likely substantially larger. <!--\textcolor{red}{[PLACEHOLDER: estimate of \emph{ex post} disaster relief spillover to be added.]}-->

[^fiscal-nfip]: The `r n_post_claims` claims for MH built 1994-1999 are observed over loss years 1994-2023. This calculation assumes no change in claim frequency or policy take-up and applies the main-specification payment reductions to the observed claim count.

This paper contributes to several literatures. First, it provides direct evidence on the returns to building code regulation for disaster resilience. @simmons_economic_2018 and @dehring_coastal_2013 study whether building code reforms in Florida for site-built homes improved resilience to hurricanes and find conflicting results. For manufactured housing, my results support a body of descriptive work examining the 1994 HUD code reform [@simmons_manufactured_2008; @kevin_r_grosskopf_manufactured_2005].

Methodologically, @baylis_mandated_2021 implement a similar study of wildfire building codes in California and find large benefits to mandatory adaptation, with fiscal spillovers and insurance value potentially justifying tighter building codes even in areas with moderate wildfire risk. This paper improves on their empirical strategy by exploiting the fact that manufactured homes are regulated federally, allowing me to disentangle building code reforms from general vintage effects. Specifically, I compare site-built and manufactured homes in the same area, exposed to the same floods, and built in the same year. My design builds on the set of methodologies used in the economics literature to study building codes, which generally rely on across-vintage or across-location comparisons [@jacobsen_are_2013; @levinson_how_2016]. My approach can be applied to any context where different housing types are subject to different regulatory bodies.

I also contribute to a rich literature evaluating the fiscal position of the National Flood Insurance Program and the broader fiscal consequences of natural disasters. My results suggest that HUD code reforms had moderate fiscal spillovers on the NFIP through reduced payouts on post-1994 MH claims, and likely larger spillovers on \emph{ex post} disaster relief programs that serve the largely uninsured MH population [@solomon_optimal_2026].

The scope of this paper is limited to only one channel of benefits -- flood damage reduction -- and does not attempt to estimate other benefits (e.g., wind damage reduction, spillovers to adjacent homes, reduced displacement, fiscal spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster assistance). I leave the estimation of these channels to future work.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{institutional-background} describes the institutional background and the 1994 HUD Code reform. Section \ref{data} describes the data. Section \ref{empirical-strategy} presents the empirical strategy. Section \ref{results} reports the results, and Section \ref{conclusion} concludes.

# Institutional Background

## Manufactured Housing and the HUD Code

Approximately 6% of the housing stock are manufactured homes. This share is substantially higher in rural areas and in the Southeast, where the share of MH can exceed 15%.[^mh-stats] These homes are disproportionately occupied by low-income households, and they are disproportionately exposed to natural disaster risk. In 1992, Hurricane Andrew destroyed 97% of manufactured homes in its path in Dade County, Florida, compared to 11% of site-built homes.[^florida-case]

[^florida-case]: *Florida Manufactured Housing Ass'n v. Cisneros*, 53 F.3d 1565 (11th Cir. 1995).

[^mh-stats]: Manufactured-Housing Consumer Finance in the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2014. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/manufactured-housing-consumer-finance-in-the-u-s/. Manufactured homes are built in a factory and transported to a site, as distinct from site-built (stick-built) homes constructed on location.

The vulnerability of manufactured homes to extreme weather prompted a major regulatory response. In 1994, HUD revised the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards---the federal building code governing all manufactured housing---to impose wind resistance requirements. The reform created a three-zone wind classification system and required structural upgrades for homes sited in high-wind zones, including stronger anchoring and strapping, upgraded sheathing and fastening schedules, and wind-pressure requirements for components and cladding. Unlike local building codes for site-built homes, the HUD Code is a federal minimum standard that preempts state and local regulation.

The preemption of local codes is a distinctive feature of the manufactured housing market. Site-built homes are subject to state and local building codes, which vary substantially across jurisdictions and are enforced through local permitting and inspection processes. Manufactured homes, by contrast, must meet a single federal standard. This institutional feature is central to the identification strategy: the 1994 reform was implemented through the federal HUD Code for manufactured homes, with wind-resistance requirements varying by HUD wind zone, while site-built homes remained governed by state and local codes. The reform was national in administration but not uniform in intensity---the binding upgrades applied to units sited in zones II and III---and the cost design in Section \ref{empirical-strategy} exploits exactly that differential exposure.

## NFIP and Flood Insurance for Manufactured Homes

The National Flood Insurance Program provides federally backed flood insurance to property owners in participating communities. Flood insurance is mandatory for properties with federally backed mortgages in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs). The requirement turns on the lending channel and the covered security property rather than on the label attached to the financing. Manufactured homes are frequently financed with chattel loans (personal property loans secured by the home but not the land), many of which fall outside the federally regulated or federally connected lending that triggers mandatory purchase. Reduced exposure to the mandate is one reason NFIP take-up among manufactured homeowners is substantially lower than among site-built homeowners in comparable flood zones.

The NFIP data used in this paper record claims and policy information at the individual level. This allows direct comparison of flood damage outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes conditional on holding NFIP coverage. The selection into flood insurance coverage is a potential concern that I address through composition checks on the insured population in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}.

# Data

## Property Transactions and the Housing Stock {#data-corelogic}

I measure manufactured home prices and quantities at the county level with property records from CoreLogic. The records consist of two files. The first is a 2023 snapshot of recorded parcels, with each parcel's county, original construction year, land use, and an indicator for whether the parcel contains a manufactured home. The second records deed transfers, with the sale date and price. I classify a parcel as a manufactured home if the indicator is set. I classify a parcel as site-built if it is recorded as a single-family residence, the indicator is not set, and its land use is not a mobile-home lot or park. Parcels in manufactured-home parks and parcels with multiple buildings or units are excluded. A manufactured home on land its owner does not hold, such as a rented park lot, is usually titled as personal property and is not a separate parcel. The records therefore cover mainly manufactured homes on land held by the owner of the home.

The price sample consists of arm's-length sales from 2000 through 2023 of homes with original construction years 1989 through 1999. A sale enters the sample if its price is positive, it is not flagged as a multi-parcel, partial-interest, or related-party transfer, it is not flagged as a foreclosure or short sale, no other transfer of the parcel is recorded on the same day, and it occurs no earlier than January 1 of the construction year. Prices include land and are deflated to 2000 dollars with the CPI-U. The construction window ends in 1999 because Florida adopted tie-down standards in that year that exceeded the federal standard. The price sample contains `r cl_n_mh_sales` sales of manufactured homes and `r cl_n_sb_sales` sales of site-built homes.

The quantity measure counts parcels in the 2023 snapshot by county, construction year, and housing type, whether or not they sold. These counts are surviving homes: a home built in 1990 and destroyed or removed before 2023 is not counted. A count therefore combines the number of homes built and the share of them that survived to 2023. The static quantity sample contains `r cl_n_mh_homes` manufactured homes and `r cl_n_sb_homes` site-built homes built from 1989 through 1999, in the `r cl_n_cty_q` counties with at least one manufactured home built in that window.

Each county is assigned its HUD wind zone under 24 CFR \S 3280.305 (Figure \ref{map:windzone-counties}). Zones II and III are treated; Zone I is the comparison. Every Florida county is in Zone II or Zone III. Outside Florida, the Zone III counties are in Louisiana and North Carolina. Alaska and Hawaii are excluded.

## Flood Damage and Insurance Coverage

I use two datasets from FEMA on individual flood insurance claims and policy records. Claims data record the date of loss, construction year, building and contents damage amounts, NFIP payments, property characteristics, and the census tract. Policy data record coverage amounts, premium, property characteristics, and flood zone designation. Both datasets include a field identifying manufactured homes.

### Final Sample

I restrict the sample to homes with construction years between 1985 and 2002 and loss years from 1994 through 2023. The sample ends in 2002 because the 2001 Florida Building Code took effect in March 2002.[^fl-standards] The take-up designs of Section \ref{appendix-take-up} use construction years 1984 through 1999, the years for which the housing-stock denominator is defined. I further restrict both the claims and policy data to detached single-family residential properties, using the occupancy classification recorded in each dataset; this excludes multi-unit residential buildings and non-residential structures from the site-built comparison group, and non-residential manufactured homes from the manufactured-home group, using the same classification on both sides. Because insurance claims and policies for manufactured homes are relatively rare, the event studies bin construction years into three-year periods: 1985--1987, 1988--1990, 1991--1993, 1994--1996, 1997--1999, and 2000--2002. The construction-year window is chosen so that 1991--1993 is the last pre-reform bin and every bin contains three full construction years. The take-up designs bin construction years into two-year periods. Cell-level policy specifications bin loss years into five-year periods; claim-level specifications use loss years. The window also matches the range over which the housing-stock denominator of Section \ref{appendix-take-up} is defined.

[^fl-standards]: Florida's earlier amendment of its manufactured-home installation rules applies within the sample. Effective March 31, 1999, Florida amended its manufactured-home installation rules (Fla. Admin. Code r. 15C-1.0104, ``Installation Standards for Anchors and Tie-downs''), imposing statewide anchoring and tie-down requirements---prompted by the destruction of mobile homes in Hurricane Andrew---that exceed the federal installation standards. \url{https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/florida/Fla-Admin-Code-Ann-R-15C-1-0104}

For the policy analysis, I construct a balanced panel at the census tract $\times$ calendar-period $\times$ housing-type $\times$ construction-period level, which I aggregate to the county level for estimation. Policy records begin in 2009, so the policy panel spans the three five-year calendar periods 2009--2013, 2014--2018, and 2019--2023; claims are assigned to the same calendar periods, so a single period index serves both. Each cell reports the number of policy-years observed during the period along with the policy-weighted average of their characteristics. A policy-year is one policy term, assigned to the calendar year containing the midpoint of its coverage period; a home insured continuously for all five years of a period therefore contributes five policy-years to that cell. The panel is balanced over housing type and construction period within tract-periods that have positive policy exposure, so cells with zero claims but at least one policy-year are retained and contribute a zero to the claim rate. Cells with zero policy-years have no defined claim rate or average policy characteristics and are excluded from those outcomes. The per-home analysis in Section \ref{take-up-results} instead uses a frame of positive-stock county, vintage, and housing-type cells crossed with calendar periods. Cells with zero policies are retained because their home-year exposure is positive; Section \ref{appendix-take-up} describes this construction.

The policy-composition results of Section \ref{selection-and-composition} use a separate extract of the same underlying policy data, at the level of the individual policy term rather than aggregated to the tract-period cell, restricted to the same construction-vintage window, calendar periods, and single-family residential occupancy classification described above.

All nominal values are deflated to constant (2000) dollars using the CPI-U. I restrict both samples to the continental US. Table \ref{tab:sumstats-nfip} reports summary statistics for the NFIP data by construction vintage and housing type. Manufactured homes generally experience lower building and contents damage than site-built homes, with correspondingly lower coverage amounts. I observe `r n_mh_claims` claims for manufactured homes in the sample, or roughly `r mh_claim_pct`% of all claims, substantially lower than the share of manufactured homes in the overall housing stock \citep{genz_why_2001}.

# Empirical Strategy

## Cost Estimation {#cost-estimation}

The 1994 standard raised the wind requirements for manufactured homes built for Zone II and Zone III counties and left them unchanged for Zone I counties. I compare manufactured homes of different construction years across counties in different wind zones. Let $c$ index counties, $s(c)$ denote the state of county $c$, $\nu$ denote the original construction year, and $t$ denote the sale year. Let $Z^{II}_c$ and $Z^{III}_c$ indicate that county $c$ is in Zone II or Zone III.

For a sale $i$ of a manufactured home, the price event study is

\begin{equation}
\ln P_i = \alpha_{c(i),t(i)} + \lambda_{s(c(i)),\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \left( \beta^{II}_k Z^{II}_{c(i)} + \beta^{III}_k Z^{III}_{c(i)} \right) \mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] + \varepsilon_i,
\label{eq:es-cost-price}
\end{equation}

where $P_i$ is the real sale price, $\alpha_{c,t}$ is a county $\times$ sale-year fixed effect, and $\lambda_{s(c),\nu}$ is a state $\times$ construction-year fixed effect. The county $\times$ sale-year effect absorbs local housing-market conditions at the time of sale. The state $\times$ construction-year effect allows each state its own vintage profile of manufactured-home prices, including depreciation and state-specific credit or demand conditions associated with construction cohorts. The coefficient $\beta^{II}_k$ is the difference in log price between Zone II and Zone I counties for manufactured homes built in year $k$, relative to the same difference for homes built in 1993; $\beta^{III}_k$ is defined in the same way for Zone III. Because the sales occur from 2000 onward, these coefficients measure differences in the resale value of existing homes, not differences in the price of new homes at placement.

For quantities, let $N_{c\nu}$ denote the number of surviving manufactured homes in county $c$ with construction year $\nu$. The quantity event study is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{E}[N_{c\nu}] = \exp\left( \alpha_c + \lambda_{s(c),\nu} + \sum_{k \neq 1991} \left( \beta^{II}_k Z^{II}_c + \beta^{III}_k Z^{III}_c \right) \mathbf{1}[\nu = k] \right),
\label{eq:es-cost-quantity}
\end{equation}

where $\alpha_c$ is a county fixed effect. The quantity event study covers construction years 1986--1999 and normalizes the zone contrasts to 1991, before Hurricane Andrew. The static count specifications retain the 1989--1999 window. I estimate Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity} by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood on a panel that contains every construction year for each county in the quantity sample, with zero counts retained. The coefficients are differences in log counts relative to 1991.

The identifying assumption is that, absent the standard, the vintage profile of manufactured-home prices (or counts) would have been the same across wind zones within a state. State $\times$ construction-year fixed effects absorb state-specific vintage profiles that could otherwise be confounded with treatment because Zones II and III are concentrated in coastal states. The main dynamic figures use this specification. Identification comes from states with counties in more than one zone; Florida contributes to the Zone III versus Zone II contrast because it has no Zone I county. I also estimate a specification with a common construction-year effect $\lambda_\nu$ in place of $\lambda_{s(c),\nu}$, reported alongside the state-specific specification in the static tables.

The static specifications replace the construction-year interactions with $\theta^{II} \, \text{Post}_\nu Z^{II}_c + \theta^{III} \, \text{Post}_\nu Z^{III}_c$, where $\text{Post}_\nu = \mathbf{1}[\nu \geq 1994]$. The standard took effect in July 1994, so the 1994 construction year is a mixture of homes built before and after it; I code it as post-reform, which attenuates the static estimates toward zero. I report six static price specifications and two specifications for each quantity outcome, numbered as the columns of Table \ref{tab:cost-static}. Column (1) uses county $\times$ sale-year fixed effects for prices (county fixed effects for quantities) and common construction-year fixed effects. Column (2) is the static version of Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-price} or \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity}, with state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects.

For prices, column (3) adds log living area and log lot size to column (2). Columns (4)--(6) add site-built homes as a second comparison within each county. Let $m \in \{\text{MH}, \text{SB}\}$ denote housing type and let $\text{MH}_i$ indicate a manufactured home. For prices, column (4) is

\begin{equation}
\ln P_i = \alpha_{c(i),t(i),m(i)} + \mu_{c(i),\nu_i} + \lambda_{m(i),\nu_i} + \theta^{II} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} \text{MH}_i Z^{II}_{c(i)} + \theta^{III} \, \text{Post}_{\nu_i} \text{MH}_i Z^{III}_{c(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
\label{eq:ddd-cost}
\end{equation}

where $\alpha_{c,t,m}$ is a county $\times$ sale-year $\times$ housing-type fixed effect, $\mu_{c,\nu}$ is a county $\times$ construction-year fixed effect, and $\lambda_{m,\nu}$ is a housing-type $\times$ construction-year fixed effect. The county $\times$ construction-year effect absorbs any difference between homes of one construction year and another within a county that is common to manufactured and site-built homes, such as a local construction boom or the location of a cohort of homes within the county. The coefficient $\theta^{III}$ is the post-1994 change in the log price gap between manufactured and site-built homes in Zone III counties, relative to the same change in Zone I counties. Column (5) replaces $\lambda_{m,\nu}$ with a state $\times$ housing-type $\times$ construction-year fixed effect, so that each state has its own vintage profile for each housing type. Column (6) adds log living area and log lot size to column (5), allowing both size coefficients to differ by housing type. The controls use positive, finite areas from the 2023 snapshot, with no upper trimming or imputation. Because these measures need not describe the home at sale and may respond to the regulation, the adjusted coefficients condition on observed size rather than measure the total price effect. For quantities, columns (3) and (4) instead replicate columns (1) and (2) using surviving site-built homes as the outcome, on the same county universe. Each housing type is estimated separately by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with zero cohorts retained. This allows substitution into site-built housing rather than assuming it is an unaffected comparison group; counties with no site-built homes in the construction window are omitted by the estimator.

For prices, columns (4)--(6) rest on a different assumption from columns (1)--(3). They allow Zone II and Zone III counties to have their own vintage profiles, provided those profiles are common to manufactured and site-built homes. They require that, absent the standard, the vintage profile of the gap between manufactured and site-built homes would have been the same across zones. In all specifications, standard errors are clustered by county, the level at which wind zones are assigned.

## Benefit Estimation: Event Study

The primary benefit-side specification is an event study that imposes no functional form on the vintage profile:

\begin{equation}
Y_{it} = \alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_m + \lambda_{\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1991} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] \times \text{MH}_i) + \varepsilon_{it}
\label{eq:event-study-benefit}
\end{equation}

where $Y_{it}$ is the outcome for claim $i$ (e.g., building damage), $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ is a county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect absorbing location-specific storm severity, $\delta_m$ is a manufactured housing indicator absorbing time-invariant differences between housing types, $\text{MH}_i$ is an indicator for manufactured homes, and $\nu_i$ is the three-year construction bin of home $i$, indexed by its first year. The term $\lambda_{\nu_i}$ is a full set of construction-vintage fixed effects common to both housing types, so that the interactions are identified off deviations from the common vintage profile rather than off the level of that profile. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore capture the manufactured-home-specific vintage profile relative to the omitted construction bin 1991--1993, the last pre-reform bin. Post-1994 coefficients are reduced-form cohort effects of exposure to the reform: because construction vintage is a proxy for actual regulatory exposure, the earliest post-reform cohorts are potentially attenuated by production-installation lags and incomplete compliance.

Identification relies on a parallel trends assumption in the vintage profile of outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes in the absence of the HUD code reform. In other words, homes built at different times may experience different levels of flood damage due to changes in construction quality, storm severity, or intra-county location, but these vintage effects should be the same for manufactured and site-built homes. I support this assumption by showing flat pre-trends in the event study specification across a broad range of claim-level and cell-level outcomes.

I expect the cohort effects to grow with later construction cohorts as compliance rates increase. Because of lags between production and installation, some units with post-1994 installation dates may have been manufactured before the regulation went into effect in July of 1994.

The cell-level specifications replace the county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect in Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit} with a county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effect, since the cell panel is aggregated to five-year periods, and omit the 1991--1993 construction bin; regressions are weighted by the number of policies in the cell. The policy panel is described in Section \ref{data}.

# Results {#results}

## Cost Side: Manufactured Home Prices and Quantities {#cost-results}

Figure \ref{fig:es-cost-price} plots the coefficients $\beta^{II}_k$ and $\beta^{III}_k$ of Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-price} with state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects. Before 1994, the 95\% interval of every coefficient in both zones contains zero. From 1994 onward, every Zone III point estimate is positive, though only the 1994 coefficient has a 95\% interval that excludes zero. The Zone II coefficients change sign across construction years, and every interval contains zero.

The dashed lines in Figure \ref{fig:es-cost-price} are HUD's \emph{ex ante} forecast of the private benefit of the standard, expressed as a log price gap between post- and pre-reform vintages: `r hud_fc_z2` in Zone II and `r hud_fc_z3` in Zone III. The forecast is the present value of reduced private wind losses, mortality, and injury, `r cl_hud_private` per home in Zone III, divided by the mean transaction price of pre-reform vintages in each zone. The comparison rests on the following argument. Homes built to the pre-reform standard cannot be built after 1994, so their supply is fixed. New homes are supplied at their cost of production, which the standard raised in Zones II and III. If a buyer regards a pre-reform and a post-reform home as equivalent apart from the resilience the standard adds, the price of a post-reform home equals the price of a pre-reform home of the same age plus the present value the buyer places on that resilience. The coefficients $\beta^{II}_k$ and $\beta^{III}_k$ therefore estimate the capitalized value of the standard to buyers, not its cost. The cost increase raises the prices of both vintages in the treated counties, and the county $\times$ sale-year effect absorbs it. If buyers place no value on the added resilience, the coefficients are zero and all manufactured-home prices in the treated counties rise by the cost increase. The gap in dollars does not depend on the value of the land, so the forecast is scaled by the full transaction price.

Every 95\% interval from 1994 onward, in both zones, contains the forecast. In Zone III, `r cl_es_p_z3_zero` of the six post-reform intervals also contain zero. Two departures from the argument above change the expected coefficient. First, a home sold at a later age has fewer remaining years of benefits, so the capitalized value, and the expected coefficient, decline with age at sale. Second, the standard raised the cost of every new home by a similar dollar amount, which lowers the relative price of larger and better-equipped homes. A shift of post-reform placements toward such homes raises the coefficient above the capitalized value of resilience. The size-adjusted specifications below address the second departure.

Panel A of Table \ref{tab:cost-static} reports the static price estimates. In column (1), the post-1994 change in the log price of manufactured homes in Zone III counties, relative to Zone I counties, is `r lad_b("price", 1, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 1, 3)`), a difference of `r lad_pc("price", 1, 3)`. With state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects in column (2), the estimate is `r lad_b("price", 2, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 2, 3)`). Adding living area and lot size in column (3) gives `r lad_b("price", 3, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 3, 3)`). Column (4) compares manufactured homes with site-built homes of the same construction year in the same county and gives `r lad_b("price", 4, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 4, 3)`). Column (5), which allows each state its own vintage profile for each housing type, gives `r lad_b("price", 5, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 5, 3)`). Adding size controls in column (6) gives `r lad_b("price", 6, 3)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 6, 3)`). Across the four specifications without size controls, the Zone III estimates range from `r lad_min("price", 3)` to `r lad_max("price", 3)`. The 95\% interval of each of these four estimates contains the HUD forecast of `r hud_fc_z3`; `r cl_static_p3_zero` of the four also contain zero.

The adjusted columns use fewer observations because they require both area measures. To distinguish sample availability from adjustment, I also estimate columns (2) and (5) on exactly the observations retained in columns (3) and (6), respectively. On the common DiD sample, the Zone III estimate is `r size_common_pc(3, 3)` without size controls and `r lad_pc("price", 3, 3)` with them. On the common triple-difference sample, it is `r size_common_pc(6, 3)` without controls and `r lad_pc("price", 6, 3)` with them. Both adjusted Zone III estimates remain positive, but neither is distinguishable from zero at the 5% level.

To express these log-price estimates in dollars, I multiply $\exp(\hat\theta^{III})-1$ by the mean transaction price of Zone III manufactured homes built in 1989--1993, `r cl_price_base` in 2000 dollars. The baseline estimate implies a premium of `r cl_premium`; across the four specifications without size controls, the dollar equivalents range from `r cl_premium_lo` to `r cl_premium_hi`. The mean uses the matched transaction sample before fixed-effect singleton removal and weights each sale equally. These are illustrative resale premiums for the home and land, not estimates of the incremental cost of producing a new home. The range describes variation across specifications, not a confidence interval; the Zone III coefficients in columns (2) and (4) are not distinguishable from zero at the 5% level.

The Zone II estimates are `r lad_b("price", 1, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 1, 2)`) in column (1) and `r lad_b("price", 2, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 2, 2)`) in column (2); adding size controls gives `r lad_b("price", 3, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 3, 2)`). The triple-difference estimates are `r lad_b("price", 4, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 4, 2)`) in column (4), `r lad_b("price", 5, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 5, 2)`) in column (5), and `r lad_b("price", 6, 2)` (standard error `r lad_se("price", 6, 2)`) with size controls in column (6). Site-built homes are subject to state and local building codes, so their vintage profiles can differ across states for reasons unrelated to the manufactured-home standard. Differences between the adjusted and unadjusted columns can also reflect the availability of size data.

Figure \ref{fig:es-cost-quantity} plots the coefficients of Equation \eqref{eq:es-cost-quantity} for surviving manufactured homes, with state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects and 1991 as the reference cohort. The expanded 1986--1999 window separates Hurricane Andrew in August 1992 from the HUD code reform in July 1994. In Zone III, the 1992 and 1993 point estimates are positive and their 95\% intervals include zero. The estimate turns negative in 1994, but its interval still includes zero; every estimate from 1995 onward is negative with an interval excluding zero. The Zone III coefficients from 1995 onward lie between `r cl_q_z3_lo` and `r cl_q_z3_hi` log points. Earlier Zone III coefficients are positive, with the 1987 interval excluding zero, so the longer pre-period does not establish a flat vintage profile. In Zone II, only the 1995 coefficient has a 95\% interval entirely below zero. The timing is consistent with a decline following implementation rather than an immediate decline after Andrew, but does not rule out delayed responses to hurricane risk.

Panel B of Table \ref{tab:cost-static} reports the static count estimates. Columns (1) and (2) use manufactured homes as the outcome. The Zone III effects are `r lad_pc("count", 1, 3)` and `r lad_pc("count", 2, 3)`, respectively; the Zone II effects are `r lad_pc("count", 1, 2)` and `r lad_pc("count", 2, 2)`. Columns (3) and (4) repeat these specifications with site-built homes as the outcome. With common vintage effects, the site-built estimates are `r lad_pc("count_sb", 3, 2)` in Zone II and `r lad_pc("count_sb", 3, 3)` in Zone III. With state $\times$ vintage effects, they are `r lad_pc("count_sb", 4, 2)` and `r lad_pc("count_sb", 4, 3)`, respectively, and neither is distinguishable from zero. These estimates provide no precise evidence of substitution into site-built homes, but their uncertainty does not rule out increases sufficient to absorb substantial manufactured-home displacement.

The counts measure homes that survived to 2023, so a change in the count combines a change in the number of homes placed and a change in the share that survived. Two forces are expected to raise the survival of post-1994 homes in Zone II and Zone III counties relative to pre-1994 homes: the pre-1994 homes were built to the weaker standard, and they have been exposed to hurricanes for more years. Either force raises the post-1994 count relative to the pre-1994 count, so it works against the estimated decline. The state-level placement estimate in Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs} is close to zero. That design assigns treatment to whole states, and most manufactured homes in treated states are sited in Zone I counties (Appendix \ref{appendix-windzone-intensity}). The quantity effects are consistent with Census 2000 counts of occupied manufactured homes by construction vintage, which do not depend on the CoreLogic parcel records; Appendix \ref{appendix-census} reports these estimates.

## Benefit Side: Flood Damage

### Post 1994 MH experience lower flood damages

Figure \ref{fig:es-building-damage} presents the event study for building damage per claim. Every coefficient is a proportional change in expected damage, for reasons given below. The omitted bin is 1991--1993, so each coefficient is measured against the three construction years immediately before the reform. The two pre-1994 coefficients are small and indistinguishable from zero. Beginning with the 1994 construction cohort, manufactured homes experience lower building damage relative to site-built homes, averaging `r bldg_dmg_evt_avg` across the three post-reform construction bins (1994--1996, 1997--1999, and 2000--2002). The coefficient for the 1994--1996 bin is not significant, the 1997--1999 coefficient is significant at the 5% level, and the 2000--2002 coefficient is significant at the 1% level. The magnitude grows across bins, consistent with the expected increase in compliance and installation practice for later cohorts. Because manufactured-home claims are few, individual bins are imprecise, and the static comparison below pools them.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static} collapses this vintage profile to a single pre/post-1994 comparison: manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim than site-built homes of the same vintage (coefficient `r bldg_dmg_lp`, standard error `r bldg_dmg_se`). Applied to the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean of `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim, this is a reduction of `r bldg_dmg_eff`. I report the static estimate as the headline number, since it is a single precisely-estimated average treatment effect rather than an average of seven individually-noisy event-study coefficients; the event study itself remains the vehicle for showing the vintage profile.

Section \ref{appendix-triple-diff} adds counties in wind Zone I, where the 1994 standard left the wind requirement unchanged, as a further comparison group. The post-1994 reduction in building damage is largest in Zone III and smallest in Zone I.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes} presents supplementary outcomes on insurance payments and damage to the building's contents. Contents damage declines by `r cont_dmg_pct` (coefficient `r cont_dmg_lp`, standard error `r cont_dmg_se`), contents payments by `r net_cont_pct`, and net building payments by `r net_bldg_pct`, consistent with improved structural integrity. Because the four outcomes are proportional changes in quantities with different means, the ordering among them in percentage terms is not the ordering in dollars: net building payments fall by a smaller percentage than building damage but from a large base, while net contents payments fall by the largest percentage from the smallest base. Policy limits and deductibles break the link between a loss and the amount the program pays, which is why the payment columns and the damage columns need not agree.

### Why the estimates are proportional

All four claim-level outcomes are estimated as proportional changes rather than as dollar differences. This choice determines the sign and size of the estimates, so this subsection states the reason.

The vintage effect these outcomes share is proportional, not additive. Manufactured and site-built homes differ in replacement cost by a factor of roughly two and a half. Any common force that changes damage by a percentage---a construction-cost trend, a change in what floods do to a house of a given quality---therefore changes it by different dollar amounts for the two housing types. A specification in dollars asks a single housing-type fixed effect to absorb a gap that is proportional, which it cannot do, and the treatment coefficient absorbs the residual. The size of the problem is not hypothetical. On simulated claims built with a treatment effect of exactly zero, but with the proportional housing-type gap and vintage gradient these data display, the dollar specification returns a large and statistically significant negative coefficient while the Poisson specification returns zero. The two specifications also disagree on the real data by about the margin that exercise predicts: the dollar estimate for building damage is `r bldg_dmg_lvl` (SE `r bldg_dmg_lvl_se`), while the proportional estimate applied to the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean is `r bldg_dmg_eff`. The gap between those two figures is the misspecification, not a finding.

Among proportional specifications I use Poisson regression rather than a regression on logged damage. Three properties matter. Poisson admits zeros natively, which the payment outcomes require: `r zero_pmt_bldg` of claims record a zero net building payment and `r zero_pmt_cont` a zero net contents payment, so a log specification would drop them and would estimate the damage and payment columns on different samples. It requires no retransformation, so the estimate can be stated without an assumption about the shape of the loss distribution. Most importantly for what follows, Poisson models the conditional mean directly, so the exponentiated coefficient is a ratio of expected dollar losses. Multiplying an observed mean by it therefore recovers a dollar figure, which is what the cost-benefit calculation of Section \ref{cost-benefit} needs and what a regression on logged damage would not supply---there the exponentiated coefficient is a ratio of geometric means, and converting it into a change in the mean requires exactly the distributional assumption that the Poisson specification avoids.

The claim-level loss and payment fields are otherwise well behaved, unlike the assessed-value and replacement-cost fields discussed in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}. Net payments are bounded by the program's statutory coverage limits.

The two damage fields are not bounded and contain a small number of records far outside any plausible single-family loss, so all four outcomes are winsorized at `r winsor_cap`. The cap binds for `r winsor_n_bldg` building-damage records and `r winsor_n_cont` contents-damage records out of more than two hundred thousand, for no payment records, and for no manufactured home. It moves the proportional building-damage coefficient from `r bldg_dmg_pct_unw` to `r bldg_dmg_pct`, and the contents-damage coefficient from `r cont_dmg_pct_unw` to `r cont_dmg_pct`. Neither movement changes any conclusion. Poisson weights an observation by its fitted mean rather than by its squared deviation, so a handful of extreme records moves it less than it moves a regression in dollars. The cap is retained because the affected records are not plausible losses, not because the estimates depend on it.

## Selection and Composition {#selection-and-composition}

A concern with the vintage-based design is that post-1994 manufactured home policyholders may differ systematically from pre-1994 policyholders, and that these compositional differences rather than construction quality drive the damage results. Table \ref{tab:composition} reports event studies for five policy characteristics, estimated on individual policy terms rather than on the cell-level panel used elsewhere in this section, restricted like the claims and policy samples throughout to single-family residential properties, and using three-year vintage bins with 1991--1993 as the reference bin, the same normalization as the damage event studies.

All five outcomes are estimated by Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML), for the reasons given in Section \ref{results} for the claim-level damage and payment outcomes: the vintage effect a common force exerts on these outcomes is proportional rather than additive, and PPML models the conditional mean directly, so every coefficient in the table is a log rate ratio on the same scale regardless of the outcome's own units. This choice matters most for replacement cost. Recorded replacement cost is not bounded: its standard deviation across policy terms is more than ten times its mean, and its maximum exceeds one billion dollars for a single-family home. A specification in dollar levels lets those records dominate the fit, explaining almost none of the variance and producing an unstable vintage profile. A specification in logs fits better but drops every policy term with a zero recorded replacement cost. PPML weights an observation by its fitted mean rather than by its squared deviation, so the extreme records no longer dominate, and the outcome enters as a level like the other four. The `r repl_zero_pct` of policy terms recording an exact replacement cost of zero are still dropped, since a zero replacement cost on an insured single-family home is a recording convention rather than a measurement, independent of which estimator reads the column. Coverage amounts are additionally bounded above by the program's statutory limits, so their dispersion is modest. The two location and design indicators (elevated building, Special Flood Hazard Area) enter as 0/1 rather than rescaled to percentage points, since under PPML a constant rescaling of the outcome is absorbed by the fixed effects and leaves the estimated coefficients unchanged. All columns are therefore on the same log-point scale.

Contents coverage enters unconditionally, with policies carrying no contents coverage recorded as zero. Separating the probability of carrying any contents coverage from the amount carried conditional on carrying some gives two margins, each indistinguishable from zero after 1994. The single unconditional column reports the same finding and avoids conditioning on a variable that itself varies across vintages.

Two patterns appear. The first concerns the pre-1994 vintages, and here the profile is a set of isolated departures rather than a single trend shared across outcomes. Building coverage is significantly lower for manufactured homes than for site-built homes of the same vintage in the earliest pre-1994 bin (1985--1987) and statistically indistinguishable from zero in the bin that follows it. Replacement cost and contents coverage are indistinguishable from zero in both pre-1994 bins. The elevated-building share is marginally higher (10% level) in the earliest bin and indistinguishable from zero in the next. The share of manufactured home policies in a Special Flood Hazard Area is indistinguishable from zero in the earliest bin and marginally lower (10% level) in the 1988--1990 bin. With two pre-1994 bins and mostly insignificant coefficients, the pre-1994 profile gives little evidence of a trend toward the reference bin in any outcome.

The second pattern concerns the post-1994 vintages, which are the ones that bear on the damage estimates. Three outcomes move in a direction that would raise, not lower, expected flood damage for post-1994 manufactured homes: building coverage is higher in all three post-1994 bins (marginally significant in the first, significant at the 1% level in the last two) and rises across them, replacement cost is significantly higher in the first two post-1994 bins and marginally significant (10% level) in the third, and the share of policies in a Special Flood Hazard Area is significantly higher in all three and rises across them. Contents coverage shows no significant post-1994 shift. The elevated-building share is indistinguishable from zero in the first post-1994 bin, marginally significant (10% level) in the second, and significant at the 1% level in the third.

These post-1994 shifts work against the main result. Higher building coverage and higher replacement cost mechanically raise the payment a given flood can generate, and concentration in Special Flood Hazard Areas raises flood exposure itself; all three would tend to increase measured damage for post-1994 manufactured homes, not lower it. The elevated-building share is the one shift that works in the direction of the main result. Its timing matters: it is absent in the 1994--1996 bin and appears in the two later bins, so elevation cannot account for the damage reduction estimated for the first post-reform cohort, and it can bear on the interpretation only of later cohorts. For those cohorts elevation is plausibly part of the treatment channel---the HUD Code encouraged improved siting and installation practices---rather than a confound.

I therefore read the post-1994 composition of insured manufactured homes as shifting toward higher, not lower, expected flood damage, and read the damage estimates as understating the effect of construction quality by whatever amount that shift contributes. This reading now rests on three outcomes moving together in the same direction rather than one, and I still do not treat it as a quantitative bound.

A separate concern operates through flood severity itself rather than through policy characteristics: if post-1994 manufactured homes are flooded to different depths than pre-1994 manufactured homes or than site-built homes of the same vintage, the damage reduction could reflect differential exposure rather than construction quality.

## Insurance Take-Up and Claim Frequency {#take-up-results}

Greater resilience could affect insurance participation as well as damage conditional on a claim. Newer manufactured homes may be more insurable, while self-protection can reduce demand for costly insurance \citep{ehrlich_market_1972}. I examine these margins using policies per home and claims per policy. Both are estimated by Poisson regression with exposure offsets and the same fixed-effect structure as the claims specifications. The home-stock denominator is imputed from Census 2000 counts of manufactured and single-family homes, adjusted for vacancy and allocated across construction years. Section \ref{appendix-take-up} provides the imputation details. Positive-stock cells with no policies enter the policies-per-home regression; claims per policy requires positive policy exposure.

Table \ref{tab:take-up-static} reports the static estimates. The post-1994 contrast in policies per home is `r tk_stc_pct` (coefficient `r tk_stc`, standard error `r tk_stc_se`), with a 95\% interval of `r tk_ci_lo` to `r tk_ci_hi`. Claims per home also increase (coefficient `r ch_stc`, standard error `r ch_stc_se`). Claims per policy change by `r cr_stc_pct` (coefficient `r cr_stc`, standard error `r cr_stc_se`), with a 95\% interval of `r cr_ci_lo` to `r cr_ci_hi`.

These results support greater NFIP take-up among owners of newer manufactured homes without a detectable increase in claim frequency among insured homes. They provide no evidence that the reduction in damage per claim is explained by selection toward homes that file fewer claims. Unchanged claim frequency does not, however, rule out selection on the severity of losses conditional on a claim. Improved insurability is one possible explanation for greater participation, but these estimates do not distinguish changes in eligibility or access from changes in insurance demand. Their causal interpretation also depends on the stock-allocation and vacancy assumptions discussed in the appendix.


# Discussion

## Cost-Benefit

The price estimates measure the value buyers place on the resilience the standard added, not its cost (Section \ref{cost-results}). At the mean transaction price of pre-reform-vintage manufactured homes in Zone III counties, the baseline resale premium is `r cl_premium`, with a range of `r cl_premium_lo`--`r cl_premium_hi` across specifications. The flood benefits below are one component of this value.

To align the geography of costs and benefits, this comparison uses the Zone III flood estimates underlying Table \ref{tab:hud-comparison}. The proportional estimates are applied to Zone III pre-1994 manufactured-home mean building and contents losses and the pre-1994 insured claim rate. Holding frequency fixed, discounting at `r hud_rate`, and assuming a `r hud_life`-year home life yields `r cl_flood_pv` per insured home in present-value avoided damage. These are the discount rate and lifespan used by HUD \citep{dacquisto_housing_2006}. The Zone III loss estimates allow the post-1994 manufactured-home change to differ by wind zone; they are distinct from the pooled main-specification loss estimates reported in Section \ref{results}.

Avoided damage and the household's private benefit differ because NFIP payments cover part of the loss. On the same pre-reform baseline, reduced payments have a present value of `r cl_public_pv` per insured home. Subtracting these fiscal savings from avoided damage gives `r cl_retained_pv` in retained-loss benefits for the insured household. Adding private and fiscal benefits recovers avoided damage without double counting. The aggregate fiscal calculation in the introduction instead applies the main-specification payment effects to observed post-1994 claims and their mean payments; it poses a different counterfactual.

The calculation holds this claim rate fixed across vintages, and Section \ref{take-up-results} reports the corresponding claim-frequency estimate. Claims per policy-year for post-1994 manufactured homes differ from the pre-1994 rate by `r cr_stc_pct` (standard error `r cr_stc_se` in log points), relative to site-built homes of the same vintage and against a pre-1994 rate of `r clmrate_base` claims per 1,000 policy-years. The estimate is not distinguishable from zero, and its exposure is observed policy-years rather than imputed home-years. Its sample is nevertheless restricted to the same supported construction years and county-types as the take-up analysis. The calculation attributes the measured benefit to severity reductions while holding frequency fixed; the confidence interval does not establish that the frequency effect is exactly zero.

Avoided flood damage is `r cl_flood_share` of the baseline resale premium, with a range of `r cl_flood_share_lo`--`r cl_flood_share_hi` across the four price specifications without size controls. Retained-loss benefits, the part of avoided flood damage that accrues to the owner, are `r cl_private_share` of the baseline premium. Under the argument of Section \ref{cost-results}, the remainder of the premium reflects other private benefits, such as reduced wind damage, displacement costs, and consumption risk, or sampling error: the column (2) interval contains zero. These are point-estimate comparisons, not confidence intervals or estimates of the social benefit-cost ratio.

Table \ref{tab:hud-comparison} compares HUD's Zone III forecasts with this paper's Zone III estimates in 2000 dollars per home. Panel A reports the cost of the standard. HUD forecast a production cost increase of `r cl_hud_resource` and a consumer price increase of `r cl_d("hud_price")` under 56\% pass-through. The vintage comparison estimates neither, because the cost increase raises the prices of pre- and post-reform homes alike. Panel B reports the capitalized private value of resilience. HUD's forecast of this value is its forecast of private benefits, `r cl_hud_private`. The estimated resale gap is `r cl_premium` in column (1) of Table \ref{tab:cost-static}, with a 95\% interval of `r cl_premium_ci_lo` to `r cl_premium_ci_hi`, and `r cl_premium_2` in column (2), with a 95\% interval of `r cl_premium_2_ci_lo` to `r cl_premium_2_ci_hi`. Both intervals contain HUD's forecast, and the second contains zero. The retained flood benefit, `r cl_retained_pv`, is one component of this value; HUD's forecast covers wind losses and does not include it. Panel C reports public benefits, which accrue to the government rather than to the owner. Panel D reports the change in surviving manufactured homes in Zone III. Under the argument of Section \ref{cost-results}, placements fall if and only if the cost increase exceeds the value buyers place on the added resilience. HUD's forecasts set private benefits equal to production cost, a ratio of `r formatC(get_cl("hud_private_cost_ratio"), format = "f", digits = 2)`, which implies no change in placements. The estimated decline in surviving homes therefore indicates a larger cost increase, a lower private value, or both, relative to HUD's forecasts. Benefits in the estimated column condition on NFIP coverage; transaction prices mainly cover manufactured homes on owner-held land. Matching the wind zone does not make these populations identical.

Extrapolating the flood benefits beyond insured homes requires an assumption about selection into NFIP coverage. Standard adverse selection would imply that insured manufactured homes face greater flood exposure than the average manufactured home, overstating the population benefit. Conversely, NFIP take-up is correlated with income, and low-income residents who are less likely to purchase coverage may occupy sites with greater flood exposure, implying the opposite sign of selection [@landry_flood_2011].

Social returns may be yet greater for two reasons. First, the code change caused fiscal spillovers on FEMA via both changes in NFIP payments and FEMA's \emph{ex post} disaster relief, predominantly provided through its Individual Assistance program. Reduced damage to post-1994 manufactured homes reduces these federal outlays, though I do not estimate effects on ex post relief directly.[^fiscal-spillover]

[^fiscal-spillover]: \cite{solomon_optimal_2026} study how changes in insurance take-up (rather than damages) affect relief spending. In principle, FEMA's individual assistance relief does not cover towards insured losses, and they find this borne in the data: an additional 1% of houses that are insured lowers ex post government spending by $175-$203 per house-flood.

# Conclusion

Manufactured homes built after the 1994 HUD wind standard sell at resale premiums of `r lad_min("price", 3)`--`r lad_max("price", 3)` in Zone III relative to earlier vintages, equivalent to `r cl_premium_lo`--`r cl_premium_hi` at the mean transaction price of pre-reform homes in those counties (2000 dollars). Because pre-reform homes are in fixed supply and are close substitutes for post-reform homes, the premium measures the value buyers place on the added resilience rather than the cost of the standard. The premium is positive in every specification but imprecisely estimated: its 95\% interval contains HUD's \emph{ex ante} forecast of private benefits, `r cl_hud_private`, in every specification and contains zero in `r cl_static_p3_zero` of four. Zone II shows no robust price premium. Surviving manufactured-home counts fall in both treated zones, which implies that the cost of the standard exceeded the value buyers placed on it. Among NFIP-insured claimants, post-1994 manufactured homes experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage and `r cont_dmg_pct` lower contents damage per claim in the pooled specification. For Zone III, present-value avoided flood damage is `r cl_flood_pv`, of which the insured household retains `r cl_retained_pv` after accounting for reduced NFIP payments. These figures leave wind benefits and other sources of value unmeasured.

For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes---disproportionately low-income, credit-constrained, and underinsured---these findings bear on where mandated adaptation is warranted. The dollar value of avoided damage scales with the value of the structure, while the cost of structural upgrades depends more on its size. Manufactured homes are worth little, so a given proportional reduction in damage is worth little in dollars, and a low-value structure in a high-risk location limits the loss its owner can suffer. Few manufactured homes carry NFIP coverage, so the mandate does not offset a large distortion created by public flood insurance. The main remaining case for the mandate is fiscal: disaster relief transfers part of the benefit of resilience from owners to the government. HUD forecast reduced federal relief of `r cl_hud_public` per home in Zone III, and this paper does not estimate that channel. The flood estimates are also measured among NFIP-insured claimants, who are likely more selected and more financially connected than the uninsured manufactured-home population. Subject to these caveats, the results indicate that the 1994 standard cost buyers of manufactured homes more than they valued it, and that the flood benefits it produced are small in dollars.

# Spillovers across Wind-Zone Boundaries {#appendix-corelogic-spillovers}

Manufactured-home plants may supply customers in adjacent counties assigned to different wind zones. If the higher requirements in Zones II and III change a plant's costs, prices, or product offerings, its customers in nearby Zone I counties may also be affected. Such spillovers would contaminate the comparison group used to estimate the price and quantity effects of the standard.

To reduce this concern, I exclude a doughnut of Zone I counties around the treated counties. A Zone I county is excluded if its shortest boundary-to-boundary distance to any Zone II or III county is at most 50 miles, including across state lines and water. I remove the entire county from both the price and quantity samples and retain all treated counties. This excludes `r cl_donut_n_counties` Zone I counties. Table \ref{tab:corelogic-donut-static} compares the baseline and restricted samples using the static specifications with state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects. The price specifications omit size controls.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Price and Quantity Effects Excluding Nearby Comparison Counties}\label{tab:corelogic-donut-static}
  \begin{threeparttable}
    {\small
    \input{output/corelogic/donut-comparison-20261019/static-appendix.tex}
    }
    \begin{tablenotes}[flushleft]
      \footnotesize
      \item Notes: All columns use manufactured homes built in 1989--1999 and compare construction years 1994--1999 with 1989--1993 in Zones II and III relative to Zone I. Columns (1) and (2) estimate log sale prices by OLS using 2000--2023 sales, with county $\times$ sale-year and state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects and no size controls. Columns (3) and (4) estimate surviving 2023 parcel counts by PPML, with county and state $\times$ construction-year fixed effects and zero county-vintage counts retained. Observations are transactions in the price columns and county-vintage cells in the count columns. Columns (2) and (4) exclude Zone I counties within 50 miles of a Zone II or III county, using the shortest distance between county boundaries. Coefficients are log points; county-clustered standard errors are in parentheses. $^{*}p<0.10$, $^{**}p<0.05$, $^{***}p<0.01$. Source: CoreLogic; Census Bureau county boundaries.
    \end{tablenotes}
  \end{threeparttable}

The results are broadly consistent across samples. The implied Zone III price premium changes from `r donut_pc("price", "baseline", 3)` to `r donut_pc("price", "donut", 3)`, and neither estimate is distinguishable from zero. The Zone II price estimates remain close to zero. The Zone III quantity effect changes from `r donut_pc("count", "baseline", 3)` to `r donut_pc("count", "donut", 3)` and remains precisely estimated. The smaller Zone II quantity decline attenuates from `r donut_pc("count", "baseline", 2)` to `r donut_pc("count", "donut", 2)`, with the restricted-sample confidence interval including zero. Thus, excluding nearby comparison counties preserves the large Zone III decline in surviving manufactured homes and does not reveal a larger price premium. This comparison supports the robustness of the main pattern to nearby controls, although it does not establish that spillovers are absent beyond the excluded area.

# NFIP Take-Up: Stock Construction {#appendix-take-up}

The take-up estimates in Table \ref{tab:take-up-static} divide policy counts by an imputed stock of homes of the same county, construction vintage, and housing type. Raw policy counts alone combine insurance participation with the number of homes available to insure.

## Stock construction

Census 2000 provides occupied housing-unit counts by county, broad construction-vintage bin, and structure type. I use mobile homes for the manufactured-home stock and one-unit attached or detached structures for the single-family comparison stock. Multifamily units and boats, recreational vehicles, and vans are excluded. To include vacant homes, I multiply each occupied vintage count by the ratio of all housing units to occupied housing units for the same county and structure type, calculated across all vintages. This adjustment assumes that the vacancy rate does not vary by vintage within a county and housing type. County-types with no occupied units have no observed vintage distribution and do not receive an imputed vintage stock.

Within each Census vintage bin, I allocate manufactured homes across construction years in proportion to state-year placements from the Survey of Manufactured Housing. Counties within a state receive the same annual shares. I allocate single-family homes using county-year single-family building permits, falling back to state shares when a county has no recorded permits in a bin. If the annual source provides no usable allocation, the bin is split equally across its years. These sources determine annual shares, not stock levels. A proportional undercount constant across a bin's years cancels from those shares; year-specific changes in coverage do not.

Shares are normalized over the full Census bin before restricting the construction window to 1984--1999. Thus, 1984--1989 receives only its allocated share of the 1980--1989 stock. Construction year 1994 is retained and coded as post-reform, although the July effective date makes it a mixture of pre- and post-reform homes. The final Census bin covers 1999 through March 2000; the allocation gives 2000 a three-month weight and retains only the 1999 stock.

## Counts, exposures, and specification

The sampling frame crosses every positive-stock county, vintage, and housing-type cell with the three five-year calendar periods covering 2009--2023. I attach observed policy and claim counts to this frame and set absent counts to zero. Stock is counted once per county and vintage, regardless of how many tracts report policies. Claims are counted directly from the claims sample, including locations with no observed policies. Cells with zero policies remain in the policies-per-home and claims-per-home regressions. Claims per policy requires positive policy exposure. Poisson estimation additionally removes fixed-effect groups with an outcome of zero throughout.

Home-years equal the imputed 2000 stock multiplied by the five calendar years in a period. Policy-years count policy terms. Each regression includes the logarithm of its exposure as an offset. The specification includes county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effects, a housing-type fixed effect, a post-1994 main effect, and a post-1994 $\times$ manufactured-home interaction, as in the static claims specification. No county $\times$ housing-type fixed effects are added. Standard errors are clustered by state because the annual manufactured-home allocation is shared by counties within a state.

In cells with positive policy counts, claims per home equals policies per home times claims per policy. This identity does not imply that the three fitted coefficients add: the regressions use different exposures and, where exposure is zero, different estimation samples.

## Mandatory and non-mandatory purchase

The mandatory-purchase component has a static coefficient of `r tk_mand_stc` (standard error `r tk_mand_stc_se`), compared with `r tk_nonmand_stc` (standard error `r tk_nonmand_stc_se`) for the non-mandated component. Mandated policies represent `r tk_mand_share` of pre-1994 manufactured-home policy-years. This split describes policies flagged by insurers as mandatory purchases; it does not isolate the building standard from contemporaneous changes in insurance-purchase enforcement, and incomplete reporting of the flag limits its interpretation.

## Stock timing

The denominator is a 2000 snapshot, while policy periods run from 2009 to 2023. Differential demolition, relocation, or changes in vacancy by construction vintage and housing type can make the later stock differ systematically from the imputation. State clustering allows correlated sampling error but does not correct such bias or uncertainty about the vacancy assumption. The estimates therefore describe insurance participation relative to a Census-anchored approximation of the stock, rather than a directly observed annual take-up rate.

# Wind-Zone Triple Difference {#appendix-triple-diff}

The 1994 standard raised wind-resistance requirements only for manufactured homes sited in HUD wind Zones II and III. Manufactured homes built after 1994 for Zone I counties were built to an unchanged standard. A post-1994 change in the manufactured-home damage gap that occurs in Zone I counties is therefore not caused by the wind standard. I use Zone I counties as a comparison group in a triple difference:

\begin{equation}
Y_{it} = \alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_{m,T_{c(i)}} + \lambda_{P_i,T_{c(i)}} + \beta \, (P_i \times \text{MH}_i) + \gamma \, (P_i \times \text{MH}_i \times T_{c(i)}) + \varepsilon_{it}
\label{eq:triple-diff}
\end{equation}

where $P_i = \mathbf{1}[\nu_i \geq 1994]$, $T_c$ indicates that county $c$ is in wind Zone II or III, $\delta_{m,T}$ is a housing-type effect specific to treatment status, and $\lambda_{P,T}$ is a post-1994 effect common to both housing types and specific to treatment status. The county $\times$ loss-year effect $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ absorbs the main effect of $T_c$. The coefficient $\beta$ is the post-1994 change in the manufactured-home damage gap in Zone I counties. The coefficient $\gamma$ is the additional change in Zone II and III counties. $\gamma$ identifies the effect of the standard if, absent the reform, the post-1994 change in the gap would have been the same in Zone I counties and in Zone II and III counties. This assumption is weaker than the identifying assumption of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit}, which requires the change to be zero in every county. A second specification replaces $T_c$ with separate indicators for Zone II and Zone III, with housing-type and post-1994 effects specific to each zone.

Table \ref{tab:windzone-ddd-building} reports the estimates for building damage. Column (1) is the baseline estimate of Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static}. Zone I counties account for `r wz_mh_z1_shr` of manufactured-home claims. In column (2), the post-1994 change in Zone I is `r wz_did_z1` (SE `r wz_did_z1_se`) and the additional change in Zones II and III is `r wz_ddd_tr` (SE `r wz_ddd_tr_se`). In column (3), the additional change is `r wz_ddd_z2` (SE `r wz_ddd_z2_se`) in Zone II and `r wz_ddd_z3` (SE `r wz_ddd_z3_se`) in Zone III. Equivalently, the post-1994 change in the gap is `r wz_did_z1` in Zone I, `r wz_did_z2` in Zone II, and `r wz_did_z3` in Zone III. The reduction is ordered by the stringency of the wind requirement, and the Zone I change is not distinguishable from zero. The triple-difference estimates are less precise than the baseline because each is a difference between two estimated changes. Zone III comprises `r wz_n_cty_z3` counties in `r wz_n_state_z3` states. Standard errors are clustered by county, the level at which wind zones are assigned.
