# Census 2000 Counts of Manufactured Homes {#appendix-census}

This appendix repeats the quantity design of Section \ref{cost-results} with Census 2000 counts of occupied housing units. The outcome is the number of occupied manufactured homes in a county built in a given vintage bin. The bins are 1980--1989, 1990--1994, 1995--1998, and 1999--2000 (through March), and 1990--1994 is the reference bin. Post-reform bins are 1995--1998 and 1999--2000. Census bins do not separate 1994 into pre- and post-reform homes, so the 1990--1994 bin is treated as pre-reform. The sample contains `r cen_n_counties` counties with at least one manufactured home in the four bins; Alaska and Hawaii are excluded. Counties absent from the wind-zone list are assigned to Zone I. As a comparison group, I use occupied one-unit site-built homes in the same bins.

Let $y_{cb}$ be the count of occupied manufactured homes in county $c$ and bin $b$. I estimate by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood
\begin{equation}
  y_{cb} = \exp\left(\alpha_c + \gamma_{s(c),b} + \theta^{II} Z^{II}_c \times \text{Post}_b + \theta^{III} Z^{III}_c \times \text{Post}_b\right) \varepsilon_{cb},
\end{equation}
where $Z^{II}_c$ and $Z^{III}_c$ indicate Zone II and Zone III counties, $\text{Post}_b$ indicates the post-reform bins, $\alpha_c$ is a county effect, and $\gamma_{s(c),b}$ is a state $\times$ bin effect. Column (1) replaces $\gamma_{s(c),b}$ with a common bin effect. Columns (3) and (4) use the same two specifications with occupied one-unit site-built homes as the outcome. Columns (5) and (6) use the specification of column (2) for owner-occupied and renter-occupied manufactured homes, respectively. Standard errors are clustered by county. Table \ref{tab:census-static} reports the estimates.

With common bin effects in column (1), the Zone III estimate is `r cen_pb(1, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(1, 3)`). Site-built homes also decline in the Census counts with common bin effects: `r cen_pb(3, 2)` in Zone II (standard error `r cen_pse(3, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(3, 3)` in Zone III (standard error `r cen_pse(3, 3)`) in column (3). With state $\times$ bin effects in column (4), they are `r cen_pb(4, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(4, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(4, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(4, 3)`), and neither is distinguishable from zero at the 5% level in Zone II or Zone III. In both zones, the manufactured-home estimates are larger in magnitude than the site-built estimates. The signs and the ordering of Zone III below Zone II are the same as in the CoreLogic estimates in Panel B of Table \ref{tab:cost-static}.

The decline in the Zone III count is concentrated among owner-occupied homes. The column (5) estimate is `r cen_pb(5, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(5, 3)`) for owner-occupied manufactured homes, and the column (6) estimate is `r cen_pb(6, 3)` (standard error `r cen_pse(6, 3)`) for renter-occupied homes, which is not distinguishable from zero. In Zone II the two estimates are similar, `r cen_pb(5, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(5, 2)`) and `r cen_pb(6, 2)` (standard error `r cen_pse(6, 2)`).

The Census counts differ from the CoreLogic counts in three ways. They record occupied homes in 2000 rather than parcels observed in 2023, so they are measured closer to the time of placement and are less affected by later survival. They include homes on rented sites, which may not appear as parcels with a manufactured home in property records. The post-reform window is two bins, 1995--2000, and the final bin is short. These differences make the Census estimates a check on the direction and rough size of the CoreLogic quantity decline, not a replication on the same sample.

Two alternative samples give similar Zone III estimates in column (2): excluding Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties, where Hurricane Andrew struck in 1992 (`r cen_b("noandrew", 2, 3)`), and adjusting counts for vacancy (`r cen_b("vacadj", 2, 3)`).

# State-Level Estimates from the Manufactured Housing Survey {#appendix-mhs}

This appendix reports a state-level design for the price and quantity effects of the 1994 standard. It assigns treatment by state rather than by county: a state is treated if it contains any county in wind Zone II or III, and all other states are controls. A treated state can include Zone I counties, in which the standard did not bind. Appendix \ref{appendix-windzone-intensity} reports the share of each treated state's manufactured-home stock that is sited in Zone II or III counties.

## Data and Price Index

This appendix estimates price and quantity effects from a state-by-year panel from the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS), which reports average sales prices and placement counts by state. The sample covers 1988--2004. It extends ten years past the reform so that it spans both the expansion of chattel lending for manufactured homes in the late 1990s and the contraction of that lending after 1999. The treatment group consists of states containing HUD wind zones II or III; the control group is zone I states.

Manufactured homes are placed in two sizes. A single-section home arrives as one transportable unit; a multi-section home arrives as two or more units that are joined on site. Multi-section homes are larger and more expensive: over the sample period the average real sales price is `r avg_p_single` for a single-section home and `r avg_p_double` for a multi-section home, a ratio of `r price_ratio` to one. The survey reports an average sales price for each size separately and an average across all homes placed. The all-homes average is the placement-weighted mixture of the two size-specific averages, so it rises both when prices rise and when placements shift toward multi-section homes. The multi-section share differs across states and changes over the sample period, so the all-homes average conflates price changes with changes in the size mix, and a shift in the mix would enter a difference-in-differences estimate as a price effect.

I therefore construct a fixed-weight price index. Let $p^{S}_{st}$ and $p^{D}_{st}$ denote the average real sales price of single-section and multi-section homes in state $s$ and year $t$. The index is

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \omega^{S} p^{S}_{st} + \omega^{D} p^{D}_{st},
\label{eq:price-index}
\end{equation}

where $\omega^{S}$ and $\omega^{D}$ are the shares of single- and multi-section homes among all homes placed nationally between 1988 and 1993, the six years preceding the reform. These weights are `r wt_single` and `r wt_double`, and they are held fixed across all states and all years. The index is therefore the cost of a fixed basket of homes: it changes only when the price of a size changes, and by construction no variation in the size mix, either across states or over time, can enter it. I report the index normalized so that its national 1993 value equals 100. The normalization divides the index by the single constant `r idx_base`, so the normalized and dollar-denominated versions of the index give the same estimates in different units.

Constructing the index requires both size-specific averages. The survey suppresses these for states with few placements, so the index is defined for `r n_index` of the `r n_raw` state-years in which the all-homes average is published. The excluded state-years are small states, predominantly in the control group. The quantity analysis uses these same state-years, even though placement counts are published more widely, so that the price and quantity effects are estimated on one sample and can be read together. All specifications are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993; `r n_dropped_mhs` states with no recorded shipments over that period are dropped from the sample.

## Specification

I estimate the effect of the 1994 HUD standard on manufactured home prices using a two-way fixed effects event study:

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \alpha_s + \gamma_t + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\text{year} = k] \times \text{Treated}_s) + \varepsilon_{st}
\label{eq:event-study-cost}
\end{equation}

where $P_{st}$ is the fixed-weight price index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} for state $s$ in year $t$, $\alpha_s$ and $\gamma_t$ are state and year fixed effects, and $\text{Treated}_s$ indicates states containing wind zones II or III. The 1993 interaction is omitted: with state fixed effects the full set of treated-by-year interactions is collinear with the time-invariant treated indicator. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore trace out the price difference between treated and control states relative to 1993. All MHS specifications, including this one, are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993. Standard errors are clustered by state.

## Results

Figure \ref{fig:es-price} presents the event study for the fixed-weight manufactured home price index. Prior to 1994, treated and control states follow parallel trends: the pre-treatment coefficients are small, precisely estimated, and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The index diverges after 1993, separates fully from 1995 onward, and rises through 1999. These are also the years of a rapid expansion of chattel lending for manufactured homes, which ended in 1999. Placements in treated states rise relative to control states over the same years and fall below them afterward (Figure \ref{fig:es-placements}), which is the pattern a regional expansion and contraction of credit would produce. Part of the price gap during the late 1990s may therefore reflect credit-driven demand rather than the cost of compliance.

The gap narrows after 1999 but remains positive through 2004. The average of the 2000--2004 coefficients is `r price_eff`, corresponding to `r price_pct` of the pre-reform index level of `r avg_price_tr` in treated states. Persistence beyond the lending expansion does not establish that the remaining gap measures compliance costs: regional credit conditions, repossession supply, and demand can have lasting effects. The main text therefore uses county-level wind-zone comparisons and treats these state-level estimates as supplementary evidence.

The 1994 coefficient is small relative to those that follow, and the separation appears from 1995. This is what the timing of the reform implies: the standard took effect in July 1994, so only part of that year's placements were subject to it, and lags between production and installation push further compliance into 1995. The premium persists through 2004, but its source---higher production costs, quality upgrading, regional credit conditions, or demand-side valuation---is not pinned down by the price path alone.

Because the outcome holds the size mix fixed, this estimate cannot reflect a shift in the composition of placements toward more expensive multi-section homes. Two comparisons show how much that restriction matters. First, holding the sample fixed, the all-homes average sales price yields `r price_eff_raw_cmn` against the index's `r price_eff`; valuing each state-year's actual size mix at fixed national prices, so that the mix shift is the only source of variation, yields `r price_eff_comp`, and the treated-control difference in the multi-section share after 1994 is `r share_dbl_eff` percentage points. The size mix therefore accounts for almost none of the price effect. Second, estimated on every state-year for which it is published rather than only those where the index is defined, the all-homes average yields `r price_eff_raw`. The gap between that figure and the index estimate is driven by the small states that drop out when both size-specific prices are required, not by composition.

I also find that price effects are larger for multi-section units (`r price_eff_double`) than for single-section units (`r price_eff_single`), though differential exposure to credit and demand shifts can also generate this pattern (Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type}).

HUD's prospective analysis provides a benchmark for these price effects. As reproduced in \citet[Table 4-17]{dacquisto_housing_2006}, the analysis predicted consumer price increases of \$829 and \$1,007 for single- and multi-section homes in Zone II, and \$1,177 and \$1,512 in Zone III, using a 56\% pass-through rate. These figures use the analysis's 1992 price baseline, whereas the estimates here are in 2000 dollars. An alternative with nearly full pass-through predicts increases ranging from \$1,402 to \$2,695. Comparing these forecasts with the estimated price response requires a common dollar year and weights for home size and wind-zone exposure. Such a comparison evaluates the joint predictions of accounting-based compliance costs and assumed pass-through; a discrepancy alone cannot identify which component accounts for it.

Figure \ref{fig:es-placements} shows the corresponding event study for log placements, estimated on the same state-years as the price index so that the price and quantity effects describe one panel rather than two. Collapsing the post-period to a single coefficient gives `r plc_eff` log points (SE `r plc_se`), a 95% interval of `r plc_ci_lo` to `r plc_ci_hi`. The point estimate is close to zero and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The single coefficient averages over two phases: placements in treated states rise relative to control states through 1998 and fall below them after 1999, following the expansion and contraction of chattel lending described above. The interval is wide enough to contain declines of roughly `r fmt_lp(abs(get_mhs("placements_effect_static") - 1.96 * get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se")))` log points as well as increases, so a modest decline cannot be ruled out. These state-level estimates do not distinguish valuation of improved construction from changes in credit supply or other demand shifts.

# Price Effects by Home Size {#appendix-section-type}

The fixed-weight index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} removes variation in the size mix by valuing a single national basket, but it does not report whether the reform raised the price of single-section and multi-section homes by the same amount. Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type} answers that question directly. I stack the panel so that each observation is one state, year, and home size, and I estimate the single-coefficient version of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-cost} with size-specific state and year fixed effects. Identification is therefore within home size, and the size mix cannot enter the estimate for the same reason it cannot enter the index. Observations are weighted by each state's mean 1988--1993 placements (the same base-period weight used throughout Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs}) times the national base-period share of their size, which reproduces the fixed-weight index where both size-specific prices are published and additionally retains the state-years where only one of the two is published.

Column (1) pools the two sizes and recovers the index estimate. Column (2) interacts the post-1994 treatment indicator with home size. Estimating the same contrast on each size separately, on that size's observations alone and with its own state and year fixed effects, gives identical coefficients, so the interaction is not an artifact of the shared fixed effects. The effect for multi-section homes is roughly twice that for single-section homes. Two readings are consistent with this pattern and the data here do not separate them: compliance may require more material on a larger structure, so that part of the cost scales with size, or multi-section homes may be placed disproportionately in the higher wind zones within treated states, where the binding requirements are stricter.

# Wind-Zone Treatment Intensity by State {#appendix-windzone-intensity}

The binary treatment indicator used in Appendix \ref{appendix-mhs} codes a state as treated if it contains any Zone II or III county, regardless of how much of the state's manufactured housing stock actually sits in one. This is a coarse proxy: a state can be classified treated on the strength of a single high-wind county while the bulk of its MH stock sits in Zone I. Table \ref{tab:windzone-intensity} reports, for every state with at least one Zone II/III county, the share of its 1980--2000 manufactured-housing stock located in a Zone II/III county, constructed by weighting each county's wind-zone status (24 CFR \S 3280.305, as classified in the eCFR crosswalk) by its manufactured-housing stock from the 2000 Census. Only 3 of the 11 treated states---Florida, Louisiana, and Massachusetts---have more than half of their MH stock in a Zone II/III county; pooling across all treated states, only about 30\% of the 1980--2000 MH stock sits in a Zone II/III county.
